FrMS88-f33409-d1e111.summary: Opens the single question covering distinctions 23–32 of Book 3: whether all the theological virtues existed together in the soul of Christ. The first argument for the negative holds that the theological virtues belong to man as wayfarer (viator).
claims: The theological virtues seem to be virtues of the wayfarer.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e124.summary: Supplies the minor premise of the opening negative argument: Christ was truly a comprehensor (one already enjoying the beatific vision), so virtues proper to wayfarers seem not to have been in him.
claims: Christ was truly a comprehensor.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e129.summary: Argument for the affirmative: Christ could merit, and the theological virtues are the habits by which wayfarers merit; so they seem to have been in Christ. The question thus turns on Christ's twofold status as comprehensor and wayfarer.
claims: Christ was able to merit.
The theological virtues are the habits by which wayfarers merit.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e136.summary: Sets out the plan of the question as ten articles: what a theological virtue is; how many there are; their properties; whether they are connected; whether they are essentially ordered; whether faith is compatible with evident knowledge; whether faith is in the intellect or the will; whether hope differs from faith and charity; whether the same habit of charity loves God and neighbor; whether the elicited and commanded acts of charity are the same. The articles shift the inquiry from Christ's soul to a general treatise on the theological virtues.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e163.summary: States a first opinion on what a theological virtue is: a virtue whose consideration belongs to the theologian.
claims: (Opinion reported) A theological virtue is one whose consideration pertains to the theologian.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e172.summary: Objects to the first definition: the theologian considers legal justice, which philosophers treat as a moral virtue; so not every virtue the theologian considers is theological.
claims: Legal justice is a moral virtue, yet the theologian considers it.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e179.summary: A second objection notes that the theologian also considers mercy, virginity, chastity, and poverty, which philosophers (who were not theologians) also treated. The definition is therefore refined: theological virtues are those that pertain to the theologian qua theologian, i.e. those that have God as their object.
claims: The theologian qua theologian considers God as object.
Theological virtues are those that regard God as their object.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e199.summary: First objection to the object-based definition: faith is not always about God, since we must also believe in the resurrection and the punishments of hell, which concern creatures.
claims: Faith also concerns created things such as the resurrection and hell.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e208.summary: Second objection: hope concerns creatable things, since we hope for created happiness.
claims: Hope regards created happiness.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e215.summary: Third objection: hope is always of the future, and God can never be future; so hope always regards a creature rather than God in himself.
claims: Hope is of the future, and God cannot be future.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e229.summary: Fourth objection: charity is also love of neighbor and so does not always regard God. Hence either faith, hope, and charity are not theological virtues, or 'theological virtue' must mean something other than what was said.
claims: Charity extends to the neighbor.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e240.summary: Reply to the first objection by distinguishing primary from secondary objects: faith always regards God as its proper object per se, but can bear on creatures as secondary objects, more per accidens.
claims: Faith has God as its proper, primary object.
Faith regards creatures only as secondary objects, quasi per accidens.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e249.summary: Applies the same distinction to hope: its primary object is uncreated happiness, and created happiness is only a secondary object.
claims: Hope's primary object is uncreated beatitude; created beatitude is secondary.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e256.summary: Says the remaining two objections (hope's futurity and charity toward neighbor) are answered in the same way, by the primary/secondary object distinction.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e261.summary: Raises a first doubt against the definition: if a theological virtue is one whose primary object is God, then theology itself, as a habit about God, would be a theological virtue.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e270.summary: Answers by distinguishing two senses of theology. As the habit of all infused virtues, gifts, and articles of belief, theology can be a theological virtue. As the deductive habit drawing theological conclusions from the first habit, it is not, because it is not a principle of merit.
claims: Theology as the habit of infused virtues, gifts, and credenda can be a theological virtue.
Theology as a deductive habit of conclusions is not a theological virtue, since it is not a principle of merit.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e284.summary: Second doubt: Aristotle's metaphysics is about God as an object, so it would seem to be a theological virtue.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e291.summary: Replies that metaphysics treats God not under the formal notion of deity but under the notion of being; its primary object is being. So it fails the definition.
claims: Metaphysics considers God under the notion of being, not of deity.
Being is the primary object of metaphysics.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e298.summary: Third doubt: the light of glory would seem to be a theological virtue.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e303.summary: Grants that the light of glory may be a theological virtue in a broad sense, but says it lacks the formal notion of one, which requires being a principle of merit or of meritorious acts; the light of glory is not, as was said earlier.
claims: A theological virtue strictly must be a principle of merit.
The light of glory is not a principle of merit and so is not a theological virtue in the strict sense.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e314.summary: Introduces the second article: how many theological virtues there are.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e323.summary: Answers on the authority of 1 Corinthians 13 that there are only three: faith, hope, and charity.
claims: There are exactly three theological virtues: faith, hope, and charity.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e329.summary: First objection: obedience has God as its object, and every such virtue is theological, so there are more than three.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e336.summary: Second objection: heroic virtue is the most perfect of the virtues, yet none is more perfect than the theological virtues; so heroic virtue should be counted among them, making more than three.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e343.summary: Third objection: latria, the worship of reverence shown to God alone, regards God immediately but is none of the three.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e352.summary: Fourth objection: wisdom, according to Augustine, exercises its highest act in contemplating and meditating on divine things, and contemplation regards God immediately.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e359.summary: Reply on obedience: it is not about God under the notion of deity. Its act concerns fulfilling divine (and also human) precepts, so through it the will tends toward God not immediately but in carrying out precepts.
claims: Obedience regards God only mediately, through the execution of precepts.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e370.summary: Reply on heroic virtue: it is not a special virtue alongside the others but an excessive degree of every virtue, as when temperance suffers no passion in its matter or fortitude fears nothing of death.
claims: Heroic virtue is not a distinct species of virtue but an excellent degree of any virtue.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e382.summary: Reply on latria: it concerns the sensible acts of worship (prayers, oblations, sacrifices) rather than God immediately. The virtue that regards God most immediately in such acts is charity, not latria, which is why philosophers counted latria, the due reverence to God, as a moral virtue.
claims: Latria concerns sensible acts of worship, not God immediately.
Latria is a moral virtue; charity regards God immediately in acts of worship.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e398.summary: Reply on wisdom: wisdom whose act is elicited from purely natural powers is an intellectual, not a theological, virtue, one the philosophers also recognized. The wisdom Augustine speaks of, elicited from a supernatural principle, is the virtue of charity.
claims: Naturally acquired wisdom is an intellectual virtue.
The supernatural wisdom Augustine describes is charity.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e409.summary: Introduces the third article: how many and what kind of properties the theological virtues have.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e418.summary: Lists four properties that also distinguish the theological from the moral virtues. (1) They are supernaturally infused, not naturally acquired. (2) They are in the superior portion of the soul, which with the inferior portion is not two powers but two offices of one power (Augustine): as moral virtues incline to lower things, theological ones incline to higher. (3) They do not lie in a mean between two vices, since no one can love, believe, or hope in God too much. (4) Their object and end are the same, since God is both object and end (our beatitude), whereas temperance's object (touch, venereal pleasures) differs from its end (happiness).
claims: The theological virtues are supernaturally infused, not acquired.
They reside in the superior portion of the soul, which is an office of a power, not a separate power.
They do not consist in a mean between two vices.
In the theological virtues, object and end coincide in God.
concepts: superior and inferior portion of the soul

FrMS88-f33409-d1e464.summary: Announces objections against the four properties, taken in order.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e469.summary: Against the first property: habits are generated from acts, so the same habits could be generated from acts of faith, hope, and charity, and would then be acquired, not infused.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e477.summary: Against the second property: by faith one is also inclined to lower things, such as believing in hell and its punishments.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e484.summary: Against the third property: one can believe too much or too little, e.g. believing four divine persons or only two; so faith consists in a mean.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e493.summary: Against the fourth property: every habit is ordered to its proper act as to its end, and the act of charity is not identical with its object; so charity's object is not the same as its end.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e502.summary: Reply to the first objection: faith generated or acquired from acts is not infused and so is not theological; it is a natural, acquired faith.
claims: Acquired faith, generated from acts, is natural and not a theological virtue.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e511.summary: Reply to the second objection: with respect to its primary object faith inclines to higher things, which suffices; it can incline to lower things only with respect to secondary objects.
claims: Faith inclines upward with respect to its primary object, which suffices for the property.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e520.summary: Reply to the third objection: there can be a defect in the theological virtues, namely believing something false, but not a defect relative to a mean. Believing more or fewer persons is not more or less belief about the same object, so it does not vary the credulity.
claims: The theological virtues admit defect by falsity, not by deviation from a mean.
Believing four or two persons is a different false belief, not an excess or deficiency of belief.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e532.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: the act of a virtue can be an end 'by which' (finis quo) but not the end 'for the sake of which' (finis cuius gratia); in the theological virtues the object is the end in the latter sense.
claims: The act of a virtue is a finis quo, not the finis cuius gratia.
In the theological virtues the object is the finis cuius gratia.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e539.summary: Introduces the fourth article: whether the theological virtues are connected.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e548.summary: Reports the common view of the doctors that the theological virtues are not connected, though the moral virtues are.
claims: (Common opinion) The theological virtues are not connected, while the moral virtues are.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e553.summary: First reason for the common view: all three virtues are infused only in baptism, while in other sacraments only charity is infused. Since faith and hope remain after baptism when charity is lost, they are not necessarily connected.
claims: Faith and hope can remain when charity is lost.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e562.summary: Second reason: despair can coexist with faith, since one despairing of salvation can keep the habit and even the act of faith; but despair removes hope, so faith and hope are not connected.
claims: Despair can coexist with faith while removing hope.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e573.summary: Third reason: according to the Apostle, only charity remains in heaven; so charity does not require faith and hope.
claims: Only charity remains in the patria.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e579.summary: Raises a doubt: why are the moral virtues said to be connected and the theological virtues not?

FrMS88-f33409-d1e586.summary: Reports the view some take with Aristotle: the moral virtues are connected through prudence, which as right reason about things to be done directs all of them.
claims: (Opinion reported) Moral virtues are connected through prudence as recta ratio agibilium.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e593.summary: First of several parallels showing the theological virtues should be connected on the same grounds: faith directs people in the theological virtues as prudence directs the moral ones, since without faith it is impossible to please God.
claims: Faith directs the theological virtues as prudence directs the moral ones.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e600.summary: Second parallel: as prudence is practical, faith looks to and passes into action, since according to James faith without works is dead.
claims: Faith is in some way practical, issuing in works.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e609.summary: Third parallel: virtues sharing one object seem more connected than those with diverse and disparate objects, and the theological virtues all have the same object, God.
claims: Sameness of object favors connection; the theological virtues share God as object.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e618.summary: Concludes that if the moral virtues are connected through prudence, the theological virtues would equally be connected through faith, which every theological virtue requires. But Meyronnes holds that the moral virtues are connected not through prudence but through legal justice (to be shown later), so he sees no reason why the theological virtues should not be connected, and defers the matter.
claims: On the prudence model, the theological virtues would be connected through faith.
Meyronnes holds that the moral virtues are connected through legal justice, not prudence.
He sees no reason to deny the connection of the theological virtues, but defers the question.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e645.summary: Objection: charity is the form of all the virtues, so the connection of the virtues should be judged by their relation to charity.
concepts: charity as form of the virtues

FrMS88-f33409-d1e652.summary: Replies that charity is called the form of the virtues only with respect to merit, since it makes the acts elicited by other virtues meritorious; the habits of the other virtues can truly remain without charity.
claims: Charity is the form of the virtues only as regards merit.
The habits of other virtues can exist without charity.
concepts: charity as form of the virtues

FrMS88-f33409-d1e661.summary: Introduces the fifth article: whether the theological virtues are essentially ordered to one another.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e670.summary: Reports the view that they are essentially ordered, based on the Apostle's sequence 'faith, hope, and charity'.
claims: (Opinion reported) Faith, hope, and charity are essentially ordered.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e675.summary: First counterargument: one can hope for something merely held by opinion, and opinion can exist without faith; so hope can exist without faith.
claims: Hope can rest on opinion without faith.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e682.summary: Second counterargument: the act of charity, an act of the will, precedes the acts of the other virtues because the will's act is prior among the powers' acts; so the habit of charity precedes the others, reversing the proposed order.
claims: The act of the will is prior to the acts of the other powers.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e692.summary: Third counterargument: Christ had charity but not faith and hope; so charity does not presuppose them.
claims: Christ had charity but not faith or hope.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e697.summary: Fourth counterargument: according to the Apostle charity never fails in heaven, while the other virtues will be done away with.
claims: Charity remains in heaven while faith and hope cease.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e704.summary: Meyronnes' determination: the theological virtues are not essentially ordered habits of themselves and by their nature, but only by divine ordination.
claims: The theological virtues are not essentially ordered by nature.
Their order derives solely from divine ordination.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e711.summary: Raises the first of several doubts about the virtues' corruption: whether faith is corrupted by sin.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e716.summary: Answers that no sin corrupts faith except heresy, because faith is in the intellect as its subject, not in the will, and nothing is contrary to it except heresy.
claims: Only heresy corrupts faith.
Faith is subjected in the intellect, not the will.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e725.summary: Second doubt: whether hope is corrupted by sin.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e731.summary: Answers that hope is corrupted only by despair, which is its contrary concerning the same object.
claims: Hope is corrupted only by despair.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e736.summary: Third doubt: whether charity is corrupted by sin.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e743.summary: Answers that charity is in fact corrupted by sin, but only demeritoriously.
claims: Charity is de facto lost through sin, by way of demerit.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e748.summary: Fourth doubt: why charity cannot coexist with any mortal sin while the other theological virtues can.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e755.summary: Replies that this does not follow from the nature of the habit or act of charity, which of itself could coexist with sin as faith and hope do. It follows only demeritoriously from divine ordination, because charity alone divides the children of the kingdom from the children of perdition.
claims: By its nature, charity could coexist with mortal sin.
Charity is excluded by mortal sin only by divine ordination, as demerit.
Charity alone distinguishes the children of the kingdom from the children of perdition.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e768.summary: Introduces the sixth article: whether faith is compatible with evident knowledge.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e778.summary: Reports the view that it is not: knowledge is evident and faith is not, and for the same thing to be evident and non-evident to the same intellect implies contradiction.
claims: (Opinion reported) Faith and evident knowledge of the same object are incompatible.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e785.summary: First of four counterarguments: no privation can be included in the formal notion of something positive. Faith is a positive habit, so non-evidence, which signifies a privation, is not part of its formal notion.
claims: Privation cannot belong to the formal notion of a positive habit.
Non-evidence is not of the formal notion of faith.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e796.summary: Second counterargument by parity: if science and faith were incompatible because one is evident and the other not, then science and wisdom would also be incompatible, since wisdom is through the highest causes and science is not.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e805.summary: Third counterargument: morning and evening knowledge are compatible, though morning knowledge (of things in the Word) is supernatural and evening knowledge (of things in their own genus) is not.
claims: Morning and evening knowledge coexist.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e814.summary: Fourth counterargument: intuitive and abstractive knowledge of the sun are compatible, the one of the sun present and the other of the sun absent, as when an eclipse is known.
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognition of the same object can coexist.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e823.summary: Concludes that science and faith are likewise compatible habits: faith is about God through authority, science through evident demonstration, and there is no contradiction in one object being both believed on authority and known by demonstration.
claims: Faith and science are compatible habits about the same object.
Faith rests on authority; science on evident demonstration.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e835.summary: Confirms with the practice of philosophers, who first taught disciples by authorities and later added demonstrative reasons. These reasons were meant to impress more firmly what was believed, not to destroy the belief, or the authorities would have been adduced in vain. Likewise the saints used both scriptural authorities and reasons without intending to exclude the faith that sacred authority produces. So faith and science coexist in fact, not merely in possibility.
claims: Demonstration added to belief strengthens it rather than destroying it.
Faith and science de facto coexist in the same knower.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e874.summary: First conclusion: the act of faith is compatible with the act of science, because their formal notions, evident certitude and firm adherence, are compatible.
claims: The act of faith is compatible with the act of science.
The formal notion of science is evident certitude; that of faith is firm adherence.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e883.summary: Second conclusion: the habit of faith is compatible with the habit of science, since habits are no more distinct than their acts.
claims: The habit of faith is compatible with the habit of science.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e890.summary: Third conclusion: the act of faith is compatible with the habit of science, since the act of one habit can coexist with an opposed habit, as an act of temperance with a habit of intemperance in someone newly reformed, whose acquired habits do not vanish at once.
claims: The act of faith can coexist with the habit of science.
An act can coexist with an opposed habit, since acquired habits do not recede immediately.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e906.summary: Objection: opinion is incompatible with science, and faith is a kind of opinion; so faith is incompatible with science.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e913.summary: Replies that the premise is false: one can hold an opinion about something through a probable syllogism and science about the same thing through demonstration, and neither destroys the other.
claims: Opinion and science about the same object are compatible.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e923.summary: Counter-objection: fear of the opposite (formido) seems to belong to the formal notion of opinion, which would make it incompatible with science.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e928.summary: Replies that formido is not of the formal notion of true opinion but only of false opinion, as with suspicion.
claims: Fear of the opposite belongs only to false opinion, not to true opinion.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e935.summary: Introduces the seventh article: whether faith is only in the intellect or in the will.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e944.summary: Reports the view that faith is in the will: I believe when I will and not when I do not, so the act of believing comes from the will, and a habit is in the power that elicits its act.
claims: (Opinion reported) Faith is in the will, since believing depends on willing.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e953.summary: First counterargument: willing is the act of charity, and among the theological virtues only charity is placed in the will.
claims: Only charity among the theological virtues is in the will.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e960.summary: Second counterargument: faith can exist without works but charity cannot, since, as Gregory says, love of God is never idle and does great things if it exists; so faith is not in the will as charity is.
claims: Faith can exist without works; charity cannot.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e968.summary: Third counterargument from Augustine: contemplation succeeds faith, and contemplation is in the intellect, so faith is too.
claims: Contemplation, which succeeds faith, is in the intellect.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e973.summary: Fourth counterargument: vision is the whole reward of faith, as fruition is of charity, and vision is in the intellect.
claims: Vision is the reward of faith and is in the intellect.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e980.summary: Meyronnes' determination: faith is a perfection of the intellect.
claims: Faith is a perfection of the intellect.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e985.summary: Supports the determination with four ordered triads: the powers of the soul (intellect, memory, will); the virtues (faith, hope, charity); the hierarchical acts (illuminating, purging, perfecting); and the dowries of the soul (vision, firm holding, fruition). On this correspondence, the habit of faith is in the intellect, where purgation is received and vision placed, and so on for the others.
claims: Powers, theological virtues, hierarchical acts, and dowries of the soul correspond in ordered triads.
Faith corresponds to the intellect and to vision.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1003.summary: Notes that believing is not causing the act of belief: believing is formally in the intellect, and from the will only effectively, not elicitively but by command. This explains the experience cited by the opposing opinion.
claims: Believing is formally in the intellect.
The will causes belief effectively by command, not by eliciting it.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1014.summary: Further notes that belief concerns neutral or contingent matters: one cannot be commanded to believe that the sun is square or the heavens smaller than the earth, against evident sight, but one can believe that Rome is in Italy, which is contingent, not simply necessary.
claims: The will can command belief only about matters not evident to the contrary.
Belief bears on contingent or neutral propositions.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1028.summary: Introduces the eighth article: whether hope is distinct from faith and charity.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1037.summary: Reports the common opinion that hope is distinct, since the Apostle counts faith, hope, and charity as three when enumerating the theological virtues.
claims: (Common opinion) Hope is a virtue distinct from faith and charity.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1044.summary: First counterargument: memory is not a power distinct from intellect and will, so hope, which is placed in memory, is not distinct from faith and charity.
claims: Memory is not a power distinct from intellect and will.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1051.summary: Second counterargument: illuminating reduces to purging and perfecting, since each presupposes illumination; the corresponding middle term of the triad is therefore not distinct.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1064.summary: Third counterargument: firm holding (tentio) is nothing other than vision and fruition, so the middle dowry, like hope, is not distinct.
claims: Tentio is nothing but vision and fruition.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1069.summary: Fourth counterargument: the soul has only two operations, willing and understanding, hence only two principal habits of virtue; every other theological virtue reduces to faith and charity.
claims: The soul has only two operations, understanding and willing.
All theological virtues reduce to faith and charity.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1081.summary: Reports that 'the doctor' concludes that hope signifies faith and charity taken together.
claims: (Opinion reported) Hope is faith and charity taken together.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1086.summary: Objection: a whole is greater than its part, but charity is the greatest of the three according to the Apostle, so hope cannot be a whole that includes charity.
claims: Charity is the greatest of the theological virtues.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1095.summary: Further objection: in this life charity is posterior to all the others, but if hope were a whole composed of faith and charity it would be posterior to them, since a whole presupposes its parts.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1102.summary: Reports another view: hope is the desire of supernal things.
claims: (Opinion reported) Hope is the desire for heavenly things.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1107.summary: Rejects it: hope can coexist with the opposite of desire for supernal things, namely the greatest desire and affection for earthly things.
claims: Hope can coexist with strong desire for earthly goods.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1116.summary: Resolves with the doctor's view that hope is a kind of species of faith, with faith as a genus over it. Hope differs from faith partially, not totally, by four conditions: hope concerns only future things, faith also past ones; hope concerns particulars (one's own salvation), faith universals and others' salvation; hope works by way of concupiscence (desire), faith by way of friendship; hope concerns only goods, faith goods and evils.
claims: Hope is a species of faith, with faith as its genus.
Hope concerns only the future; faith also the past.
Hope concerns one's own salvation; faith extends to universals and others.
Hope is in the mode of concupiscence; faith in the mode of friendship.
Hope is only of goods; faith of goods and evils.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1146.summary: Introduces the ninth article: whether the charity by which we love God and neighbor is the same habit.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1155.summary: Reports one opinion: there are two habits, since there are two objects and habits are distinguished by objects, as acts are.
claims: (Opinion reported) Love of God and love of neighbor are two habits.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1162.summary: First counterargument: in heaven God and creature are seen by the same act; much more can they be loved by the same habit, since acts are more incompatible than habits.
claims: In heaven God and creatures are seen in one act.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1169.summary: Second counterargument: by the same act one enjoys God and uses the creature; so by the same habit God and neighbor can be loved.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1176.summary: Third counterargument: by the same act the end and the means to the end are loved, and creatures are ordered and referred to God as their end.
claims: The end and the means are loved by one act.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1183.summary: Determination: by the same habit of charity we love God as primary object and creature as secondary object. The relation is asymmetric: we can love God by this habit without loving our neighbor, since the habit is ordered to God per se and primarily, to neighbor secondarily and quasi per accidens. But we cannot love the neighbor by it without loving God, because in essentially ordered things the second necessarily presupposes the first, and what is per accidens presupposes what is per se.
claims: One habit of charity loves God (primary object) and neighbor (secondary object).
One can love God by charity without loving neighbor, but not conversely.
In essentially ordered things, the posterior necessarily presupposes the prior.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1206.summary: Introduces the tenth article: whether the commanded act of charity is distinct from its elicited act.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1215.summary: Distinguishes the two acts of charity: the elicited act (willing), which is formally in the will, and the commanded act (moving other powers or the bodily members), which is not formally in the will but in the other powers that elicit it.
claims: Charity has an elicited act (willing) and a commanded act (moving powers or members).
The elicited act is formally in the will; the commanded act is formally in the executing powers.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1228.summary: Reports the opinion that the two are one and the same act: the commanded act is just the elicited act joined to a sensitive or other power inferior to the will.
claims: (Opinion reported) The commanded act is the elicited act conjoined to an inferior power.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1237.summary: First counterargument from Aristotle: the will rules the body and members with despotic rule, as a master rules a slave, which executes the command willy-nilly. The act by which the will so commands the members is not elicited by the will, so it differs from the elicited act.
claims: The will rules the members despotically.
The act executed in the members is not elicited by the will.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1248.summary: Second counterargument: the will rules the sensitive appetite with political rule, as a king rules princes, since the appetite drawn by pleasure does nothing unless it wills. The act of such command is not formally in the will, so it is not elicited by the will and is distinct from the elicited act.
claims: The will rules the sensitive appetite politically.
The commanded act is not formally in the will and so differs from the elicited act.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1268.summary: Raises a doubt: whether the will is a cause of the commanded act.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1274.summary: Answers that it is, since upon its act something else follows: an effect, the act of a lower power, or motion in the members.
claims: The will causes the commanded act.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1283.summary: Specifies that the will is the universal cause of the commanded act, while the power in which the act formally exists (or the member) is its particular cause.
claims: The will is the universal cause of the commanded act; the executing power is its particular cause.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1290.summary: Further doubt: then the will would seem to tend to an object not previously known, which is false, since the will tends to nothing without a prior act of intellect.
claims: The will tends to no object without a prior act of the intellect.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1299.summary: Answers by distinguishing the will's willing from its causing: by its elicited act (willing) the will tends only to a foreknown object, but by its commanded act, by which it causes something outside itself, it can bear on an object not yet known, since that effect does not yet exist.
claims: Willing (elicited act) requires a foreknown object.
Causing through a commanded act can bear on an object not yet known.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1315.summary: Raises a further doubt: whether the commanded act adds any moral goodness to the elicited act.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1322.summary: Answers no: no merely naturally elicited act can be meritorious, since it is not free but necessary, and every lower power executes by natural necessity whatever the will commands. The commanded act, being merely natural on the side of the executing power, can have no goodness beyond the will's elicited act.
claims: The commanded act adds no moral goodness or merit to the elicited act.
Lower powers execute the will's commands by natural necessity.
Only free acts can be meritorious.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1336.summary: Confirms from Christ's saying that the widow who gave two mites merited more than the rich who gave much more. She could merit more only by the interior elicited act, since the rich performed more exterior, commanded acts.
claims: Merit is measured by the interior elicited act, not the exterior commanded act.

FrMS88-f33409-d1e1349.summary: A further confirmation from the liturgy for St. Martin, also applicable to other saints: 'O blessed man… whom the persecutor's sword did not take, yet who did not lose the palm of martyrdom'. Hence the exterior act adds nothing to the interior as regards merit.
claims: The exterior act adds nothing to the interior act with respect to merit.

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e156.summary: Defines a theological virtue. Meyronnes rejects the definition 'a virtue the theologian considers', since theologians also treat moral virtues known to philosophers such as legal justice, mercy, and chastity. He replaces it with 'a virtue that has God as its object'. Objections that faith, hope, and charity also bear on creatures (the resurrection, created happiness, the future, the neighbor) are met by distinguishing God as primary, per se object from creatures as secondary, quasi-accidental objects. Three doubts then sharpen the definition: theology counts as a theological virtue only as the habit of infused virtues and articles of belief, not as a deductive habit of conclusions; metaphysics treats God under the notion of being, not deity; and the light of glory is a theological virtue only broadly, since strictly a theological virtue must be a principle of merit.
claims: A theological virtue is one whose primary object is God.
Creatures are only secondary objects of the theological virtues.
Strictly, a theological virtue must be a principle of merit.
Deductive theology, metaphysics, and the light of glory are not theological virtues in the strict sense.

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e316.summary: Establishes on the authority of 1 Corinthians 13 that there are exactly three theological virtues, and turns away four candidates for addition. Obedience regards God only mediately, through carrying out precepts. Heroic virtue is not a distinct species but an excellent degree of any virtue. Latria concerns the sensible acts of worship and is a moral virtue, while charity is what regards God immediately in worship. Wisdom is either a naturally acquired intellectual virtue or, in Augustine's supernatural sense, identical with charity.
claims: There are exactly three theological virtues.
Obedience, heroic virtue, latria, and wisdom are not further theological virtues.
Heroic virtue is a degree of virtue, not a species.
Latria is a moral virtue.

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e422.summary: Sets out four properties distinguishing theological from moral virtues: they are supernaturally infused, not acquired; they reside in the superior portion of the soul (an office of a power, not a separate power); they do not consist in a mean between two vices; and their object and end coincide in God. Replies to objections defend each property: acquired faith is not theological; faith inclines upward with respect to its primary object; faith admits defect by falsity but not excess or deficiency relative to a mean; and the act of a virtue is only a finis quo, while God as object is the finis cuius gratia.
claims: Theological virtues are infused, in the superior portion of the soul, not in a mean, and have the same object and end.
Acquired faith is not a theological virtue.
The theological virtues admit defect by error, not by deviation from a mean.
God as object is the finis cuius gratia of the theological virtues.
concepts: finis quo and finis cuius gratia

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e560.summary: Asks whether the theological virtues are connected. Meyronnes reports the common denial: faith and hope survive the loss of charity, despair removes hope while faith remains, and only charity remains in heaven. He then questions the asymmetry with the moral virtues. If moral virtues are connected through prudence, the theological virtues would be connected through faith, which directs them, is practical, and shares their single object. But since he holds that moral virtues are connected through legal justice rather than prudence, he sees no reason to deny the connection of the theological virtues and defers the question. Charity's role as 'form of the virtues' is restricted to merit: other virtues' habits can exist without charity.
claims: The common opinion denies the connection of the theological virtues.
Meyronnes holds that moral virtues are connected through legal justice, not prudence.
Meyronnes sees no reason to deny the connection of the theological virtues, though he defers the matter.
Charity is the form of the virtues only with respect to merit.
concepts: charity as form of the virtues

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e693.summary: Denies that faith, hope, and charity are essentially ordered by their own nature. Hope can rest on opinion without faith; the will's act of charity is prior among acts; Christ had charity without faith and hope; and charity alone remains in heaven. Whatever order holds among them comes from divine ordination. A series of doubts on corruption follows: faith, subjected in the intellect, is destroyed only by heresy; hope only by despair; charity is in fact lost by mortal sin, but only demeritoriously. By its nature charity could coexist with sin as faith and hope do, and it is excluded only by divine ordination, since charity alone separates the children of the kingdom from the children of perdition.
claims: The theological virtues are not essentially ordered by nature, only by divine ordination.
Only heresy corrupts faith; only despair corrupts hope.
Charity is lost through mortal sin only demeritoriously, by divine ordination, not by its nature.

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e808.summary: Argues against the view that faith is incompatible with evident knowledge. Non-evidence is a privation and cannot be part of the formal notion of a positive habit, and analogous pairs coexist: science and wisdom, morning and evening knowledge, intuitive and abstractive cognition. Faith (from authority) and science (from demonstration) are therefore compatible about the same object. The practice of philosophers and saints, who added reasons to authorities to confirm belief rather than to destroy it, shows they coexist in fact. Three conclusions follow: the acts of faith and science are compatible (evident certitude and firm adherence), so are their habits, and the act of faith is compatible with the habit of science. Opinion likewise coexists with science, since formido belongs only to false opinion.
claims: Faith is compatible with evident scientific knowledge of the same object.
Non-evidence is not of the formal notion of faith.
The formal notion of faith is firm adherence; that of science is evident certitude.
Faith and science coexist de facto, not only possibly.
Formido belongs only to false opinion.

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e983.summary: Rejects the view that faith is in the will because one believes when one wills. Willing is proper to charity; faith can exist without works, unlike charity; contemplation and vision, which succeed and reward faith, are in the intellect. So faith is a perfection of the intellect, supported by the correspondence of four triads (powers, theological virtues, hierarchical acts, dowries of the soul). The will's role is explained by distinguishing formal subject from cause: believing is formally in the intellect and caused by the will only by command, not by eliciting it. Such command extends only to contingent or neutral matters not evident to the contrary.
claims: Faith is subjected in the intellect.
The will causes belief by command, not elicitively.
Belief can be commanded only in contingent matters not evident to the contrary.

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e1084.summary: Asks whether hope is a distinct virtue. Against the common opinion grounded in the Pauline triad, arguments reduce hope to faith and charity, on the grounds that memory, illumination, and tentio are not distinct middle terms and the soul has only two operations. The 'doctor's' view that hope is faith and charity taken together fails, because charity is the greatest virtue and is posterior in this life. The view that hope is a desire for supernal things fails because hope can coexist with strong earthly desire. Meyronnes adopts the doctor's resolution that hope is a species under faith as its genus, partially distinct from it by four conditions: futurity, particularity (one's own salvation), the mode of concupiscence, and restriction to goods.
claims: Hope is not a composite of faith and charity.
Hope is not simply desire for supernal things.
Hope is a species of faith, partially distinct from it by four conditions.

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e1213.summary: Holds against the two-habit view that one habit of charity loves God and neighbor. The arguments: one act of vision sees God and creature in heaven, one act enjoys God and uses creatures, and one act loves end and means. God is charity's primary, per se object and the neighbor its secondary, quasi-accidental object. Hence the asymmetry: one can love God by charity without loving the neighbor, but not the neighbor without God, since in essentially ordered things the posterior presupposes the prior.
claims: One habit of charity loves both God and neighbor.
God is the primary and neighbor the secondary object of charity.
Love of neighbor by charity presupposes love of God, but not conversely.

FrMS88-f33409-Dd1e1281.summary: Distinguishes charity's elicited act (willing, formally in the will) from its commanded act (moving lower powers or members, formally in those powers). Against the view that they are one act, Meyronnes argues from Aristotle's despotic rule of the will over the members and political rule over sensitive appetite that the commanded act is not elicited by or formally in the will. The will is the universal cause of the commanded act and the executing power its particular cause; and while willing requires a foreknown object, causing need not. Finally the commanded act adds no moral goodness or merit, since lower powers act by natural necessity. The widow's mite and the liturgical praise of St. Martin, who kept the palm of martyrdom without the sword, confirm this.
claims: The commanded act of charity is distinct from the elicited act.
The will is the universal cause and the executing power the particular cause of the commanded act.
The will's causing, unlike its willing, need not bear on a foreknown object.
Exterior commanded acts add nothing to the merit of the interior elicited act.

FrMS88-f33409.summary: The single question on distinctions 23–32 of Book 3 asks whether all the theological virtues were together in Christ's soul. The arguments set Christ as comprehensor, who would lack wayfarers' virtues, against Christ as one able to merit through them. The question is never answered directly. Instead it becomes a ten-article treatise on the theological virtues. (1) A theological virtue is one whose primary object is God, and strictly a principle of merit; this excludes deductive theology, metaphysics (which treats God as being), and the light of glory. (2) There are exactly three, with obedience, heroic virtue, latria, and wisdom excluded or reduced. (3) They are infused, in the superior portion of the soul, not in a mean, and have God as both object and end. (4) Meyronnes reports the common denial that they are connected but, holding that moral virtues are connected through legal justice rather than prudence, sees no reason to deny their connection, and limits charity's role as 'form of the virtues' to merit. (5) They are not essentially ordered by nature but only by divine ordination; faith is lost only by heresy, hope only by despair, and charity by mortal sin only demeritoriously. Article 5 also states, in passing, that Christ had charity but not faith or hope, which bears on the opening question. (6) Faith (firm adherence on authority) is compatible in act and habit with evident science. (7) Faith is in the intellect; the will causes belief only by command. (8) Hope is a species of faith, partially distinct by four conditions. (9) One habit of charity loves God primarily and neighbor secondarily. (10) The commanded act of charity is distinct from the elicited act but adds nothing to its merit.
claims: A theological virtue has God as primary object and is a principle of merit.
There are exactly three theological virtues: faith, hope, and charity.
The theological virtues are infused, in the superior portion of the soul, not in a mean, with God as object and end.
The theological virtues are ordered only by divine ordination, not by nature.
Christ had charity but not faith and hope.
Faith is compatible with evident scientific knowledge of the same object.
Faith is subjected in the intellect; the will causes belief by command.
Hope is a species of faith.
One habit of charity loves God and neighbor.
Exterior commanded acts add nothing to the merit of interior elicited acts.
